After segmenting teeth on 3D surface scans, I wanted to look beneath the surface. 🦷

A CBCT scan is a 3D X-ray of the jaw: bone, tooth roots, the pulp inside each tooth and the nerve canals running through the jaw. ToothFairy3 is a public dataset of 532 of these scans, labelled voxel by voxel into 77 classes, and I dug into U-Mamba2, the solution that won both tasks of the ToothFairy3 challenge at MICCAI 2025.

The video walks through a real scan:
1️⃣ A CBCT scan is a stack of slices, 262 of them here, 0.3 mm apart. Thats 68.7 million voxels, too many for a 3D network in one go, so U-Mamba2 works on 160 × 288 × 288 patches and slides across the scan.
2️⃣ Every voxel is labelled: jaws, each tooth by number, sinuses, pharynx, crowns and implants.
3️⃣ ToothFairy3 added the pulp of every tooth and three thin nerve canals. In this scan those canals cover 136 to 819 voxels each, against 1.4 million for the lower jawbone, so U-Mamba2 weights them 10× in its loss.
4️⃣ The network is nnU-Nets residual CNN U-Net with one addition. A 1 × 160 × 288 × 288 patch goes down the encoder to a 5 × 9 × 9 grid of 320-channel features. A Mamba2 layer reads that grid as a sequence of 405 tokens, carrying a small state from token to token, so features pick up context from across the patch, not just their neighbourhood. The decoder brings it back up to 47 class scores per voxel, and the argmax gives the label.

One thing stood out to me:
🔹 Domain knowledge did a lot of the work. The architecture change is a single layer. Around it: label smoothing between related structures, extra weight for tiny ones, label-aware mirroring, and removing predicted blobs smaller than almost any real one in the training labels. In the papers validation, that last step alone added 0.016 to 0.035 Dice to every model tested.

Full write-up, with architecture diagrams and an interactive 3D viewer of the scan 👇

Meet Piper, my new mobile robot!
Piper is a differential-drive mobile robot with depth vision, and soon I plan to give it its own intelligence as well.
I started building Piper a couple of weeks ago  to learn more about mobile robotics and explore Edge AI for autonomous robots.
The laptop inside the middle compartment currently acts as the robot’s main computing unit. It is also running RTAB-Map for SLAM and mapping. The 3D point-cloud map in the video is currently a bit noisy because I was intentionally driving the robot with some jerky movements and haven’t tuned the default parameters yet. 

Current architecture :
ROS 2 + micro-ROS for the robot software architecture. The ESP32 runs the micro-ROS client, which communicates with the micro-ROS Agent running on the laptop over Wi-Fi using UDP.
Planetary Geared DC motor with encoders for wheel odometry
MPU6050 IMU for improving odometry through sensor fusion
OAK-D Pro for depth perception and visual information
OAK-D Pro's onboard 9-axis IMU can also be used to improve state estimation
RTAB-Map for SLAM and 3D mapping
Visual odometry is also being performed as part of the RTAB-Map pipeline.

The next step is to improve the robot's state estimation, tune the SLAM pipeline, and start experimenting with edge AI for perception and autonomous navigation.
Still a lot to build, but Piper is starting to look like a real robot. 

Huge Thanks to my mentor Rajdeep Singh Sohal and Ishan Sehgal for their support and guidance.

🧠📝 Meta just introduced Context Language Models (CLMs) - language models that manage their own context instead of just appending to it. 🚀

But here’s the interesting part:

The model isn't just reading its context. It can rewrite it.

The context is exposed as a file, and the model edits it with plain Bash or Python - summarize, delete, reorganize, back up.

🔢 The numbers (zero-shot, no training):
→ +11.4% accuracy with 21.5% fewer FLOPs on Browse Comp-Plus
→ +5% score with 59% fewer FLOPs on 12-hour Edge Bench
→ 65% greater speedup on a 24-hour agent swarm at the same compute

🔬 What emerged on its own:
→ Progress scoreboards
→ A private “notes” chat role
→ Subagents spawned by creating a file

📈 And its learnable:
→ Evolved skills: up to +35.9 pts on ContextBench
→ RL: +47.6% for Qwen3.5-9B
→ Suffix Cache Reuse: 35% less server compute

The bigger idea:
Context engineering is moving from hand-designed rules → letting the model decide what to keep, rewrite, or forget.

What happens when models become their own context engineers? 🤔

Shoutout to Wavestone AI Lab👏

Their new paper, "Harness Engineering: Anatomy, Architecture, and Evolution of Coding Agents," reverse-engineered the source code of 11 coding agents: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenHands, Aider, OpenCode and more.

Their big takeaway: in 2026, coding agent harnesses went from tools to platforms.

OpenHands is their example. It's the one harness that can run Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI as interchangeable backends, so you're not betting your eng org on one model vendor.

A few other things they called out:

▶ Event-sourced conversation engine with a persistent event log
▶ Parallel delegation across agents
▶ Defense-in-depth security model
▶ MCP + SKILL.md support, which are fast becoming the industry standards


Thanks for the shoutout Paul Barbaste, Tristan Darrigol, Germain Vu & Tom Wiltberger

I was truly lucky to spend six years in the Jayich Lab at UCSB, surrounded by wonderful people and great facilities. I can't imagine finishing this journey without their help and support.

My personal life changed a lot, too. I met my life partner, Eunseo, and we were blessed with a priceless gift, our daughter Arlene. We've faced many uphill climbs along the way, and some are still ongoing, but we've gotten through so much together.

Now I'm starting a new chapter. I'm happy to share that I've joined Google Quantum AI as a Calibration Engineer! This has been my dream since I was an undergrad, and now it has come true. AI House Amsterdam exists for mornings like this.

The whole idea behind it is that the hardest questions in AI don't get answered by technology alone. They get answered when you put founders, leaders and the next generation in the same room and let them think out loud together.

That's what happened when UNFOLD, a community of Corporate Affairs and Communications leaders shaping the role of business in society, held its Convene at AI House. 

Unfold Co-Chair Saskia Kapinga (Shell) opened, Arent Jan (AJ) Hesselink set the theme, Leading in the Age of AI, around a simple idea: the scarce resource isn't AI, it's the judgement to use it well. Euro Beinat (Prosus) shared what deploying AI at scale across Prosus's 100-plus markets actually looks like. Charlie Pemberton (Prosus), Kim L. (ING) and Laura Peijs (Treasury) explored what it means for organisations and people, while Darryl Soh (Edelman) and Seán Earley (Teneo) brought the agency perspective.

What followed was multi-generational groups challenging whether existing ways of leading still fit, and a reminder that AI processes information but people provide the meaning.

You don't build ecosystems by broadcasting. You build them by convening. Thanks to UNFOLD and everyone who brought the room to life.

The UNFOLD community gathered at AI House Amsterdam last Friday for this year's Convene, hosted by Prosus and led by chair Anita van de Velde - Rayat and co-chair Saskia Kapinga.

Saskia opened the event before Arent Jan (AJ) Hesselink, who recently joined the UNFOLD Board, took us into the morning's theme: Leading in the Age of AI. The discussion was built around a simple idea: in this shift, the scarce resource is not the technology itself, but the judgement and leadership needed to use it well.

Euro Beinat, who leads AI across Prosus and its operations in more than 100 countries, opened with a first-hand view of deploying AI at scale. A panel with Charlie Pemberton, Kim L. and Laura Peijs explored what this shift means for organisations and people, while Darryl Soh and Seán Earley brought the agency perspective, where the pressure to adapt is often felt earliest.

The second half of the morning belonged to the room, where mixed, multi-generational groups explored what this moment means for leadership in our profession, with the NextGen Board bringing the conversations back to share with everyone.

A couple of threads carried through the morning. One was about being willing to question whether existing ways of leading and working still fit, brought into sharper focus by having different generations, who are living these decisions differently, in the same room rather than separate conversations. The other was a reminder that AI can help us process and understand information, but it still takes judgement, context and people to work out what it actually means.

A huge thank you to the team at Prosus AI House, and to Charlie Pemberton, Madeline Duncan and Rebecca Bryant, for hosting us so generously.

We left with plenty to think about, and with a shared sense that the most important questions are only just beginning.

I’ve started building a snake robot, a modular structure with multiple servo-driven joints designed for serpentine locomotion.

The current body is basically the skeleton; the head, tail and outer scales are still to come, while I’m working on the gait and joint movements.

The motion you see here is called a 𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐭, where a travelling wave moves through the joints to propel the robot forward.

Why a snake? I’ve always been fascinated by how robotics can replicate movements found in nature. Festo India bio-inspired robots have been a big inspiration for me.

This is one of the first versions that actually moves, still a long way to go, but we’re getting there. 🐍

Spent yesterday at Pragati Q-Foundry in New Delhi, organised by the National Quantum Mission (NQM). Here's how the day unfolded 👇

🔐 PQC Migration Workshop
The day opened with where Post-Quantum Cryptography stands today: why migration is needed, why it's urgent, and how industry plans to meet the 2029 target. The keynote by Mr. T V Ravichandran (Deputy NSA) and the roadmap shared by Dr. Rajkumar Upadhyay (CEO, C-DOT) set the tone.

💰 Investors' Fireside Chat
Chaired by Mr. Anupam Saronwala (IAN, ex-IBM Research), the panel shared how investors look at deep tech, quantum startups in particular, and how much long-term value they see in the space.

🇮🇳 Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh spoke about NQM's progress and India's ambition to lead the global quantum industry.

🤝 Quantum Startup Expo, the highlight of my day
I spoke with the founders at QpiAI , QuBeats , QNu Labs , and a team building silicon spin qubits, asking the same three questions: What are you building? What problems did you run into? How did you turn research into an industry-ready product?

Most conversations centred on superconducting qubits, photonic qubits and cryo-CMOS (control electronics that run at cryogenic temperatures, close to the qubits). The cryo-CMOS discussions felt especially close to home, as it's an area I've recently started exploring.

One thread kept coming up: research is only the starting point. The real story is in the problems along the way and the iterations it takes to turn a lab result into a product industry can use.

🗺️ State representatives then shared how their states are progressing in the quantum space, a reminder that this is becoming a nationwide effort.

💭 What I'm taking away
As a second-year student working on quantum hardware, seeing research, policy, capital and industry in one room, and talking to people who have taken quantum tech from lab to market, made the path feel much more real. I came back with a clearer picture of where India's quantum ecosystem is heading, and where I'd like to contribute.

Thanks to National Quantum Mission (NQM) and the organisers for a wonderful event. Grateful to have attended under the guidance of Prof. Anagh Bhaumik, Ph.D. alongside, Om Patel and Vansh Goel .

Stanford  and NVIDIA have introduced CLM-8B (Contrastive Language Model), an open-source model designed for fast decision-making in AI agents.

The key idea is simple:

Traditional LLMs generate tokens to reason and decide what to do next.

CLM focuses directly on selecting the right action.

For example, an agent has:

→ Search Customer
→ Get Order Details
→ Issue Refund
→ Escalate to Human

Given the current situation, CLM compares the current state with available actions, scores them, and selects the best match.

This enables a System 1 architecture for agents:

🧠 System 2 / LLM → Reason & Plan
⚡ System 1 / CLM → Decide & Route
🔧 Tools → Execute

CLM-8B is built around a Qwen3-8B backbone and uses contrastive learning to bring correct state-action pairs closer and incorrect pairs further apart.

Another interesting optimization: action embeddings can be cached, reducing repeated computation when the available tools remain the same.

I just want to say that I’ve seen many people commenting “Interested” under almost every job opening. Some posts don’t even say to comment “Interested,” but people still write “Interested” anyway.

And most of the time, the job post is from a different company. Everyone is just commenting “Interested,” when you can simply search that company on Google, check their careers page, and apply directly instead of commenting “Interested.”

And most of the people who tell you to comment “Interested” are actually just fooling you. They’re doing it for reach.

The genuine people actually put the job application link in the comments or in the post itself. That’s actually helpful.

So instead of just commenting “Interested,” if you’re genuinely interested in a job, just search for the company, find the careers page, and apply directly.

NVIDIA drops a new tabular foundation model(TFM) called Kumo Tabular.

If you’ve been following models like TabPFN or TabICL, the setup will look familiar. The model takes in labeled rows as context, and it predicts new rows in a single forward pass.

Kumo Tabular comes in Small, Medium, and Large versions, from about 28M to 215M parameters.

It runs through NVIDIA’s open-source structured-data-models(SDM) library. SDM is a GPU-native library for structured-data foundation models and preprocessing ans also includes models such as TabICLv2, TabFM, and KumoRelational. 

Exciting times ahead for the tabular data space.

You can read more about it in their official blog : https://lnkd.in/ggxn9Xpi
